description: Team of 3 friends, we met at the University of Bath and met back up to work on this hackathon combining all our skillsets :)
summary:
Mons Carlo answers the question every lunar mission planner asks: if we land here, on this date, with this lander, will it survive? 

We allow you to pick a site, a date and a lander. The app shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the real terrain horizon, when power and radio windows open and close, and gives an hour-by-hour verdict on the battery and radio link. 

We also added a Monte Carlo simulation of over 10,000 landings, contingency planning and ranked backup sites for launch slips. Everything runs on NASA LOLA and JPL data.

Website Link: https://mons-carlo.fly.dev/
Github Link: https://github.com/Otman-BEH/MonsCarlo
details:
Pick a site and a date. We’ve set up 16 sites, including the Artemis III candidates (de Gerlache rim and Malapert Massif), Shackleton rim, the connecting ridge that Blue Moon MK1 is aiming for, Mons Mouton (VIPER and IM-2), Malapert A (IM-1), Chang’e 7, Chandrayaan-3 and Apollo 11. You can also type in any latitude and longitude, and any date from 1900 to 2100. The next 14 months are preloaded so they’re instant.

See the Sun and Earth against the horizon. Status cards tell you how high the Sun and Earth are above the actual terrain, plus a countdown, to the second, until the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise. You can also look around a first-person view of the surface, check a 360° sky panorama showing where the Sun and Earth will travel over the next lunar day, or hit Play to watch a day go by every second.

Three maps. There’s a flat map showing day and night and where Earth can see, a south-pole shadow map cast from the real terrain, and a 3D globe. Tap anywhere on any of them to check that spot.

Power and comms. You get how much solar power your lander makes now and over time, how many hours you get sunlight and Earth in view, the longest night, the longest gap without a radio link, and which Deep Space Network stations (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) can see you.

Compare sites. Put up to five sites side by side over the same window, with matching sky charts, a table of numbers, simple yes/no timelines and a 12-month calendar of good landing dates.

Mission verdict. This runs an hour-by-hour simulation of the battery and radio link for 12 real landers, using published figures from ispace, Intuitive Machines (Nova-C), Firefly (Blue Ghost), ISRO (Vikram), Astrobotic (Griffin and Peregrine), Blue Origin (Blue Moon MK1) and the Apollo LM. You can also put in your own numbers. Anything that wasn’t published is clearly labelled as an assumption.

Landing risk, the Monte Carlo part. Real landings never touch down exactly where they’re aimed, so we simulate thousands of them scattered around the target, with uncertainty in the terrain, touchdown spot, timing and hardware. You get the chance of success (with a 95% confidence range), a heat map showing where landings work and where they don’t, the main reasons landings fail, which uncertainty matters most, and a better place to aim if there is one. This is where the team name comes from.

What if things go wrong? You can test a weaker solar array or battery, extra power draw, a lost antenna, safe mode, stricter physics and a heat model. The mission design tool works out the smallest solar array and battery that would still get you through, and how that changes with landing date.

If the launch slips. It re-ranks the other sites and landing times after a delay, which is exactly the situation the challenge describes.

For every level. There’s a 60-second guided tour, a “Why the pole?” page comparing Apollo 11 with Shackleton rim, plain-English captions on every chart, links you can share to a specific scenario, and a Method page that lists every assumption and limitation.


Why it’s useful

  • You get a go/no-go answer in seconds instead of spending hours across several expert tools.
  • It shows why a site works or doesn’t (a ridge in the way, a long night, Earth dipping behind a hill), which makes it easier for science and engineering teams to agree.
  • It’s made for plans that change: compare sites over the same window, slide the date around, or rank backups after a delay.
  • It’s upfront about uncertainty. You get confidence ranges, a terrain-margin check and flagged assumptions, and the Method page lists the limits.
  • It’s open: MIT licence, a public API, and every data file listed with its checksum and source.

What we hope to achieve

We’d like Mons Carlo to be a quick first-look tool for CLPS and Artemis planning, and a teaching tool that makes the strange lighting at the lunar south pole easy to get your head around. We’d also like it to be something other people build on through the open API, adding things like link budgets, thermal models or sharper terrain.

Tools, languages and software

  • Backend: Python 3.12 to 3.14 with FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Requests, tifffile and imagecodecs (for reading the LOLA GeoTIFFs), SpiceyPy with NAIF CSPICE, and an SQLite cache. Tests use pytest and HTTPX.
  • Frontend: plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS with no framework, Canvas 2D, and a first-person terrain view ray-cast on the CPU. Fonts are IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono and Space Grotesk.
  • Deployment: Docker on Fly.io (London), deployed from GitHub using GitHub Actions.

How it works

We take two things: where the Sun and Earth are, and what the horizon looks like from the site.

The Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, with NASA SPICE (DE440) as a backup. The horizon is traced in 720 directions, out to 330 km, from NASA LOLA elevation maps. We use the sharpest map available, down to 5 m per pixel at south-pole landing sites. Everything else (power, radio windows, the mission simulation and the Monte Carlo) comes from comparing those positions against that skyline.

All the maths runs on a Python backend, so anyone can get the same results through our public API at /docs.

How we know it’s right

We checked it against independent sources:

  • Our positions match JPL’s separate DE421 ephemeris to within 0.000015°, across 3,166 times at 6 sites.
  • It caught all five lunar eclipses between Aug 2026 and Dec 2028 on the right dates.
  • The Python engine gives the same results as our original in-browser version, and the Monte Carlo matches bit for bit
